items.prompt: What is "environment drift" most precisely?
choices: A bug in the application code that only appears under heavy load
The gradual, usually unintentional divergence of dev/CI/production environments (OS, runtime, libraries, settings) even though the source code is identical
A deliberate infrastructure migration from one cloud provider to another
Any bug that takes more than a day to reproduce
items.explanation: Drift is specifically about the *environment* diverging, not the code — three environments set up independently and patched on different schedules end up with different runtime versions, libraries, or settings, even while running byte-identical source code.
items.reference:
Same code, different environment — that gap is drift.

Why: nothing in a diff review can catch an assumption the code never wrote down.
items.learnMore:
Environment drift

Drift is the environment diverging, not the code. Each environment is set up and patched on its own schedule, so identical source code ends up running against different runtime versions, libraries, and settings.

Common mistake

Assuming drift means someone made a mistake. It's usually nobody's fault — three independent setup histories just produce three different environments.

items.prompt: A laptop, a CI runner, and a production server were each set up independently, months apart, by different processes. Nobody ever compared their installed software versions. What has almost certainly happened by now?
choices: Nothing — as long as nobody edited a config file, all three stayed identical
The three environments have drifted apart from each other, purely as a byproduct of being set up and patched on separate schedules
They can only differ if someone used a different cloud provider for one of them
Drift can only happen to production, never to a laptop or CI runner
items.explanation: Independent setup histories are exactly how drift happens without anyone doing anything wrong — a laptop's install history, a CI image's release schedule, and a production base image's patch cadence are three unrelated processes with no reason to stay in sync unless something forces them to.
items.reference:

Why: nothing in a diff review can catch an assumption the code never wrote down.

items.prompt: True or false: environment drift requires someone to have deliberately changed a configuration somewhere.
choices: True — drift only happens when a config file is edited
False — drift is usually the accumulated byproduct of independent setup and patch schedules, not any single deliberate change
True, but only for production environments
False — drift is a synonym for a deliberate infrastructure migration
items.explanation: No single deliberate change is required. Three environments installed at different times, by different processes, simply end up different — that's the whole mechanism, and it's why drift is so easy to miss until it causes a bug.

items.prompt: What's the key structural difference between a container and a VM, relevant to why containers became the default for environment parity?
choices: Containers are always faster at CPU-bound computation than VMs

A VM virtualizes an entire OS kernel per instance (heavy, slow to boot); a container shares the host kernel and only isolates the process/filesystem view (light, fast), while still packaging the full app dependency environment
Containers can only run one process ever, VMs can run many
There is no real difference; "container" is just newer marketing for the same VM technology
items.explanation: Containers trade some isolation strength (shared host kernel) for being lightweight and fast to start, while still fully packaging the app's runtime and dependencies — which is the part that matters for parity: the same bundled environment runs everywhere, regardless of isolation depth.
items.reference:
🖥️ VM

own guest kernel, boots fully

📦 Container

shares host kernel, still packages full deps

Why: parity comes from the packaged deps, not the isolation depth.
items.learnMore:
Containers vs. VMs, for parity specifically

Isolation depth and environment parity are separate properties. A VM's deep isolation isn't what buys parity — the parity guarantee comes from baking the exact runtime and dependencies into one artifact at build time, which a container does just as well as a VM while staying lightweight.

Common mistake

Thinking a container's weaker isolation means a weaker parity guarantee. They're independent axes — parity is about the packaged artifact, not the isolation boundary.

items.prompt: A colleague argues "containers can't really guarantee parity as well as VMs, since containers isolate less." What's the flaw in that argument?
choices: There's no flaw — the colleague is correct, VMs guarantee stronger parity

It conflates isolation depth with parity. Parity comes from packaging the exact runtime/dependencies into one built artifact — a property containers have just as fully as VMs, independent of how deeply either isolates the process
Containers are actually more isolated than VMs, so the premise is simply backwards
Parity is only a meaningful concept for VMs, not containers
items.explanation: Isolation and parity answer different questions: isolation is about how protected the host is from the running process; parity is about whether the same dependency environment runs everywhere. A container can have weaker isolation and identically strong parity, because parity is a property of the built artifact, not the isolation boundary around it.
items.reference:

📦 Container

shares host kernel, still packages full deps

Why: parity comes from the packaged deps, not the isolation depth.

items.prompt: Why does a container start in seconds while a comparable VM takes tens of seconds to minutes?
choices: Containers always run on faster hardware
A container shares the host's already-running kernel; a VM has to boot an entire separate guest operating system, kernel included, before anything can run
VMs always have larger disk images, which is the only reason they're slower to start
Containers skip loading the application's dependencies at startup
items.explanation: The speed gap is about what has to come up before the app can run: a container reuses the host's kernel, so starting one is closer to starting a process; a VM boots a full guest OS from scratch first.

items.prompt: A team's package.json pins "engines": { "node": "20.x" } in every environment. Does that alone guarantee environment parity?
choices: Yes — matching the runtime version in a config file is the entire definition of parity
No — parity means the OS, runtime, and dependency versions all match exactly, not just one version number declared in a config file; system libraries underneath can still differ
Yes, as long as all three environments are on the same cloud provider
No, because engines fields are ignored by every package manager
items.explanation: "Same version on paper" is necessary but not sufficient — an engines field constrains one number (the Node major version) while leaving the OS, system libraries, and everything else the code might silently depend on completely unconstrained.
items.reference: Not "similar" — the same: OS, runtime, and dependency versions, everywhere.
items.learnMore:
What parity actually requires

"Same version on paper" (e.g. both pinned to Node 20 in package.json engines) still allows OS-level library drift underneath. Real parity means the full runtime stack is identical, not just the parts a config file happens to declare.

Common mistake

Treating a matching version number in a config file as proof of parity. The OS and system libraries underneath can still differ.

items.prompt: Which best captures what "environment parity" means, as this unit uses the term?
choices: Dev, CI, and production are running roughly comparable, similarly-configured environments
Dev, CI, and production are running the exact same environment — down to OS, runtime, and dependency versions — so a whole class of 'worked here, broke there' bugs becomes structurally impossible
Every environment has the same amount of CPU and memory allocated
Every developer uses the same code editor and operating system on their own laptop
items.explanation: The word doing the work is "exact," not "similar" — parity is a strong, structural guarantee, not a rough approximation. That's what turns an entire category of drift bugs from 'possible' into 'impossible,' rather than just 'less likely.'
items.reference: Not "similar" — the same: OS, runtime, and dependency versions, everywhere.

items.prompt: Which of these is a source of environment drift that a source code diff would never reveal?
choices: A function's parameter name being renamed
A locally-installed CLI tool being at a different version than the one CI has, silently changing a build step's behavior
A new unit test being added to the test suite
A comment being updated to reflect new logic
items.explanation: A tool version installed on a machine is entirely outside the source tree — a diff review has nothing to look at, because the divergence isn't in any file the review covers, it's in what's installed on the machine running the build.
items.reference:
🕐 Timezone/locale
🔌 Free port
🧰 Global CLI tool version
📚 System library
items.learnMore:
Drift hides where nobody's looking

None of these show up in a source diff — a locale setting, a globally-installed tool version, a free port, a system library's default behavior are all ambient facts about the machine, not the code.

Common mistake

Only looking for drift in obviously "infrastructure-y" settings. Ambient state like a free port is just as real a drift source, and easier to overlook.

items.prompt: A service works fine locally but fails with a connection-refused error whenever it's run on a shared build machine. The code never changed. What kind of drift source does this most likely point to?
choices: A runtime version mismatch
Ambient state — e.g. a port the code assumes is free happens to already be occupied on the shared machine
A locale/timezone setting
A missing environment variable
items.explanation: "Connection refused, elsewhere only" is the signature of ambient state — something about what else is running on that particular machine (a port already in use) rather than a version or setting difference.

items.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a drift category to a realistic symptom?
choices: System library version → a build step behaves differently depending on who runs it
Environment variable (e.g. TZ) → date math produces different results on different machines, passing every test that doesn't cross a timezone boundary
Installed tool version → a new unit test fails to compile
Ambient state → a locale-dependent string formats differently

items.prompt: What does it mean to say a container "makes the environment part of the versioned, reviewed artifact"?
choices: It means the Dockerfile is stored in the same git repo as the app code, nothing more

It means the OS libraries, runtime, and dependencies the app needs are baked into the same built, reviewable artifact as the code itself, instead of living as separate tribal knowledge (setup notes, a wiki page) that can silently go stale
It means every container automatically gets code-reviewed before it can run
It means containers cannot be built without a formal architecture review
items.explanation: The shift is from 'the environment lives in someone's head or a doc that drifts from reality' to 'the environment is baked into the same artifact as the code, built once and never re-resolved' — that's what actually closes the parity gap, not just storing a Dockerfile in version control.
items.reference: App + OS libs + runtime + deps → one artifact, run everywhere unchanged.
items.learnMore:
The environment as a versioned artifact

The core shift containers make: instead of the environment being tribal knowledge (setup notes, a wiki page), it's baked into the same reviewed, versioned artifact as the code itself.

Common mistake

Treating a setup README as equivalent to a container image. A README can go stale the day after it's written; a built image can't drift from itself.

items.prompt: A team maintains a detailed "local setup guide" wiki page instead of a container image. Why is that a weaker parity guarantee, even if the guide is accurate today?
choices: It isn't weaker — a sufficiently detailed wiki page provides identical guarantees to a container image

The guide describes what someone should install, but nothing enforces that every environment actually followed it or stays in sync as it changes — a container image is what was actually installed, baked in, and identical wherever it runs
Wiki pages cannot describe software versions
The guide is weaker only because wikis are slower to load than Docker images
items.explanation: A guide is a description someone has to follow correctly, every time, and keep updated forever; an image is the actual result, already baked in — one is a set of instructions that can be followed incorrectly or go stale, the other is a fact about what's actually there.
items.reference: App + OS libs + runtime + deps → one artifact, run everywhere unchanged.
items.learnMore:

The core shift containers make: instead of the environment being tribal knowledge (setup notes, a wiki page), it's baked into the same reviewed, versioned artifact as the code itself.

Common mistake

Treating a setup README as equivalent to a container image. A README can go stale the day after it's written; a built image can't drift from itself.

items.prompt: Why does a parity-focused Dockerfile use `npm ci` instead of `npm install`?
choices: npm ci is faster in every case, with no other difference
npm ci refuses to proceed if package-lock.json doesn't exactly match package.json, guaranteeing the exact locked dependency tree instead of silently re-resolving slightly different versions
npm install doesn't work at all inside Docker containers
npm ci automatically updates the lockfile to the latest compatible versions
items.explanation: npm install can resolve a slightly different dependency tree if the registry state has shifted since the lockfile was generated; npm ci fails loudly instead of silently drifting — exactly the guarantee a parity-focused build step needs, since a silently different node_modules tree is itself a form of environment drift.
items.reference:
npm install

can re-resolve transitive versions

npm ci

fails loudly on any lockfile mismatch
items.learnMore:
Why the build step's install command matters for parity

A silently different node_modules tree between two builds is itself a form of drift, even with identical source and an identical lockfile on disk. npm ci removes that risk by refusing to proceed instead of quietly resolving something close-but-different.

Common mistake

Assuming an unchanged package-lock.json guarantees an unchanged install. npm install can still resolve differently if registry state shifted; npm ci is what actually pins it.

items.prompt: Two builds of the same commit, a week apart, both use `npm install` against an unchanged package-lock.json. Can they produce different `node_modules` trees?
choices: No — an unchanged lockfile always guarantees an identical install, regardless of which install command is used
Yes — npm install can resolve slightly different transitive versions if registry state shifted in that week, which is exactly the drift npm ci is designed to prevent
No, because npm caches every install result forever by default
Yes, but only if the Node.js version also changed
items.explanation: npm install isn't guaranteed to reproduce byte-for-byte the same resolution from an unchanged lockfile if the registry itself has changed underneath it — this is precisely the class of silent drift npm ci exists to close off, by refusing to proceed instead of resolving something slightly different.
items.reference:

can re-resolve transitive versions

npm ci

fails loudly on any lockfile mismatch

items.prompt: package.json and package-lock.json have gone out of sync (someone hand-edited one without updating the other). What does `npm ci` do that `npm install` would not?
choices: npm ci silently fixes the mismatch by regenerating the lockfile
npm ci fails the build immediately with an error, rather than proceeding with a best-effort resolution
npm ci deletes package.json and rebuilds it from the lockfile
There's no difference; both handle the mismatch identically
items.explanation: npm ci's entire purpose is to be strict where npm install is forgiving: a mismatch between the two files is exactly the kind of ambiguity npm install would try to resolve around, while npm ci treats it as a build-breaking error — surfacing the problem immediately instead of shipping an image built from an ambiguous dependency state.

items.prompt: The Dockerfile copies `package.json`/`package-lock.json` and runs `npm ci` BEFORE copying the rest of the source code. What's the practical benefit of that ordering?
choices: It's required — Docker will error if you copy source code before dependencies
Docker layer caching means `npm ci` only reruns when the dependency manifests actually change, not on every source code edit, making rebuilds much faster
It reduces the final image size by roughly half
It has no real effect; the ordering is purely stylistic convention
items.explanation: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a cached layer keyed on its inputs. Putting the rarely-changing dependency install before the frequently-changing source copy means most rebuilds (just source edits) skip the expensive `npm ci` step entirely and reuse the cached layer.
items.reference:
Source copied first

install reruns on every edit

Manifest + install first

source edits skip install
items.learnMore:
Layer order affects speed, not correctness

Both orderings produce a correct, parity-preserving image — the difference is purely how often the expensive install step has to rerun during active development, since Docker's cache key for a layer depends on the layer before it plus that layer's own inputs.

Common mistake

Confusing this with a parity issue. It's a build-speed issue — both orderings produce an equally parity-correct final image, they just cost differently to rebuild.

items.prompt: If a Dockerfile instead copied the entire source tree BEFORE the dependency manifests and `npm ci`, would the resulting image still achieve environment parity?
choices: No — parity requires the manifest-first ordering, or the dependency versions won't be pinned correctly
Yes — the final image contains the same pinned dependencies either way; the ordering only affects how often the expensive layer has to rebuild during development, not what ends up in the image
No — copying source first causes npm ci to install a different set of packages
Yes, but only if the image is rebuilt from scratch every single time
items.explanation: Parity is about what the final image contains, and both orderings end up with the same npm ci run against the same lockfile — the ordering is purely a caching/rebuild-speed concern, completely orthogonal to whether the resulting artifact is parity-correct.

install reruns on every edit

Manifest + install first

items.prompt: What does a layer's Docker cache key actually depend on?
choices: The current date and time of the build
The output of the previous layer, plus that layer's own instruction and the content of any files it copies in
A random value regenerated on every build
Only the instruction text, never any file contents
items.explanation: Content-based hashing chained from the previous layer is exactly what makes the cache both correct and predictable — a layer reuses its cached result only when everything it actually depends on (the prior layer's output plus its own inputs) is provably unchanged.

items.prompt: In the `build_image`/`run` pseudocode model, why does `build_image` running exactly once per release matter for parity?
choices: It doesn't matter — parity comes from the Dockerfile's content, not from how many times it's built

Because every additional independent build is another chance for dependency resolution or a base image patch to differ, even from unchanged source — running it once and distributing the result removes that risk entirely
It matters only for reducing CI compute costs, not for correctness
build_image must run once because Docker only allows a single build per repository
items.explanation: Every time install() runs, it's a fresh opportunity to resolve differently — a registry change, a base image patch. Building once and distributing that exact result (rather than rebuilding per environment) is what removes that opportunity from every environment except the single build.
items.reference: build_image() runs once. run() executes the same result everywhere.
items.learnMore:
Why "build once, run everywhere" is the whole mechanism

The moment any environment re-runs its own install/build step, it can independently drift from the others — even from an unchanged source tree, because dependency resolution or a base image patch can differ by the time it runs. Doing it once and distributing the result removes that possibility entirely.

Common mistake

Thinking "every environment builds from the same Dockerfile" is equivalent to parity. It isn't — each build can still independently resolve differently; only distributing one already-built artifact removes that risk.

items.prompt: A team has every environment (dev, CI, prod) independently run `docker build` from the same Dockerfile, rather than building once and distributing the image via a registry. Does this achieve the same parity guarantee?
choices: Yes — as long as the Dockerfile is identical, every build produces byte-identical results, so it doesn't matter how many times it's built

No — each independent build is a fresh opportunity for dependency resolution or a base image patch to differ, even from unchanged source; parity requires distributing one already-built artifact, not rebuilding it per environment
Yes, because Docker builds are guaranteed to be deterministic by design
No, but only because rebuilding is slower, not because of any correctness concern
items.explanation: An identical Dockerfile doesn't guarantee an identical build result, because the base image tag can resolve to a newer patch, or the dependency registry can have shifted — this is exactly the gap `run` never has to worry about, precisely because it never re-resolves anything.
items.reference: build_image() runs once. run() executes the same result everywhere.
items.learnMore:

Common mistake

Thinking "every environment builds from the same Dockerfile" is equivalent to parity. It isn't — each build can still independently resolve differently; only distributing one already-built artifact removes that risk.

items.prompt: In the pseudocode model, what does `run(image)` explicitly NOT do that `build_image` does?
choices: run() never starts an actual process, only build_image does
run() never calls install() or resolves any dependency — everything it needs is already baked into the image it was handed
run() rebuilds the image from source every time it's called
run() only works for images built on the same machine it's running on
items.explanation: run() is deliberately "dumb" — it starts a process against an already-fully-resolved filesystem. That absence of any install/resolve step inside run() is exactly what makes it safe to call on any number of machines without risking drift.
items.reference: build_image() runs once. run() executes the same result everywhere.

items.prompt: A report generator produces different date labels on two machines with the same code and the same input. Which drift category does this match, and why is it "invisible until it breaks"?
choices: Runtime version — because only a Node version bump could ever affect date formatting
Environment variable (TZ) — the divergence lives in an ambient setting neither machine's test suite happens to exercise unless a test crosses a timezone boundary
Installed tool version — because date libraries are considered CLI tools
It can't be drift at all, since the code and input are identical
items.explanation: Identical code and identical input, different output, is precisely the signature of an ambient environment variable driving the divergence — it passes every test that doesn't happen to straddle the specific condition (here, a timezone boundary) that exposes it.

Matching a symptom back to its drift category

Recognizing which category a bug belongs to is what turns "mysterious flake" into "known class of problem with a known fix" — an env-var-shaped bug and a runtime-version-shaped bug get diagnosed completely differently.

Common mistake

Treating every "worked here, broke there" bug as the same kind of mystery. The table's categories each have a distinct signature once you know to look for it.

items.prompt: A service works fine when run alone on a CI runner but fails with "connection refused" only when run in parallel with another job on a shared build machine. Which drift category best explains this?
choices: Ambient state — the port the service assumes is free is already occupied by the other concurrently-running job on the shared machine
Runtime version — a Node version mismatch is the only thing that can cause connection-refused errors
System library — a missing OS package causes this specific error message
This cannot be drift, since the service passes when run alone
items.explanation: The tell is that it only fails under a specific concurrent condition (another job sharing the machine) — that's ambient state, not a version or setting difference, and it's exactly why this category is so easy to miss: it's invisible until two things happen to collide on the same machine.

items.prompt: Reading the `build_image`/`run` pseudocode literally: which line is the ONLY place dependency resolution happens at all?
choices: `image.add(app_source)`
`image.install(dependency_manifest)` inside build_image
`start_process(image, isolated=True)` inside run
Dependency resolution happens in both build_image and run, once each
items.explanation: `install()` is called exactly once, inside `build_image` — `run()` never touches dependency resolution at all, it just starts a process against a filesystem that's already fully resolved.
items.reference:
build_image(): install() runs once
run(): no install, ever
items.learnMore:
Reading the build/run pseudocode

build_image's install() call is the only place dependency resolution happens at all. run() never resolves anything — it just starts a process against an already-fully-baked filesystem, which is exactly what makes it safe to call run() on as many machines as you want.

Common mistake

Assuming run() does some lightweight re-check of dependencies. It does none — that's the entire point of separating build from run.

items.prompt: Why is it safe, in the pseudocode model, to call `run(image)` on an unlimited number of different machines without risking drift?
choices: Because run() re-downloads dependency_manifest fresh on every call, guaranteeing the latest versions everywhere
Because run() performs no installation or version resolution at all — it only starts a process against a filesystem that build_image already fully resolved once
Because Docker automatically synchronizes every running container's filesystem in real time
It isn't actually safe; parity still requires re-running install() on each machine to be sure
items.explanation: Safety here comes from what run() deliberately doesn't do: no re-resolution, no re-installation. Whatever install() produced once inside build_image is exactly what every run() call executes, everywhere, unchanged.
items.reference:
build_image(): install() runs once
run(): no install, ever

items.prompt: A team containerizes their app and declares "environment parity solved." Two weeks later, a bug reproduces in staging but not production because the staging database has an out-of-date schema migration. Was the container's parity guarantee violated?

No — the container guarantees parity for what's inside it (OS, runtime, app dependencies); a database schema is outside the container's boundary and needs its own parity mechanism (e.g. migrations run consistently in every environment)
Yes, because the database driver version is part of the container image
No, because database bugs are never really environment-related
items.explanation: Per L3's failure modes, container parity doesn't automatically propagate to systems outside the container — a schema drift is a real parity failure, just at a different layer (the database), which needs its own explicit consistency mechanism rather than being covered for free by containerizing the app.

Yes, because all external API behavior is technically part of environment parity by definition

items.prompt: Implement the fixed `isToday(timestampMs, timezone, referenceNowMs)` from L3: instead of relying on the host machine's ambient local timezone (which drifts between dev/CI/prod), it must format both timestamps in the SAME explicitly-passed IANA timezone (e.g. "UTC", "America/New_York") using `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, and compare the resulting date strings.

tests.description: in UTC, this pair falls on different calendar days
the SAME pair, evaluated in America/New_York, falls on the same calendar day

items.explanation: Formatting both timestamps through the same explicit `timezone` parameter removes any dependence on the host machine's ambient local timezone setting — the function now produces the identical answer no matter which machine (laptop, CI runner, production host) executes it, because the timezone is part of its explicit input rather than inherited silently from the environment.
items.reference: Format both timestamps through the same explicit timezone — never read the host's ambient clock setting.
items.learnMore:
Removing an ambient dependency

Date.getFullYear/getMonth/getDate all silently read the host's local timezone. Intl.DateTimeFormat with an explicit timeZone option removes that ambient read entirely, so the function produces the same answer regardless of which machine runs it.

Common mistake

Fixing this by setting TZ=UTC everywhere instead. That's still an ambient setting someone has to remember to set correctly on every machine — the real fix removes the dependency from the code.

items.prompt: The Dockerfile pins `FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim` — a specific version tag, not `latest`. Does this alone guarantee byte-for-byte reproducibility across every build?
choices: Yes — a specific version tag can never be repointed to different content
Not quite — a tag, even a specific one, is technically still a mutable pointer a registry maintainer could repoint; true byte-for-byte reproducibility requires pinning by content digest
No, because Docker ignores version tags entirely and always pulls the newest image
Yes, but only for official Docker Hub images, never for private registries
items.explanation: A specific tag like 20.11-bookworm-slim is far more stable in practice than latest, but it's not cryptographically guaranteed immutable the way a content digest is — production pipelines that need true byte-for-byte reproducibility pin by digest (`@sha256:...`) on top of the tag.
items.reference:
Tag: node:20.11-bookworm-slim — can be repointed.
Digest: @sha256:... — cannot.
items.learnMore:
Tag pinning vs. digest pinning

A specific version tag is far more stable in practice than latest, but it's still technically a mutable pointer a registry maintainer could repoint. A content digest is derived from the actual bytes, so it can only ever refer to one exact image.

Common mistake

Treating a version-numbered tag as an absolute guarantee. It's a strong practical convention, not a cryptographic one — only a digest is truly immutable.

items.prompt: What's the practical difference between `FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim` and `FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim@sha256:9f2c...`?
choices: There is none; the digest suffix is purely decorative and ignored by Docker
The tag alone can, in rare cases, be repointed to different content by the registry; the digest suffix pins to the exact bytes, so that reference can never resolve to anything else
The digest form only works for private registries, never for Docker Hub
The tag form is faster to pull, the digest form is slower, with no other difference
items.explanation: The digest is a hash of the actual image content — appending it means the reference can only ever resolve to those exact bytes, closing the (rare but real) gap that a tag alone leaves open.
items.reference:

Digest: @sha256:... — cannot.

items.prompt: When does the difference between tag pinning and digest pinning actually matter in practice?
choices: Never — the distinction is entirely theoretical and has no real-world consequence

When true byte-for-byte reproducibility is required (e.g. security-sensitive builds, strict compliance auditing) — for most teams, a specific version tag is a reasonable and much simpler practical compromise
Only when using `latest` as the tag, in which case digest pinning becomes irrelevant
Only for images larger than 1GB
items.explanation: This is a genuine trade-off, not a strict "always use digests" rule — a specific version tag is a reasonable practical choice for most teams, while digest pinning earns its extra complexity when the stakes (security auditing, strict reproducibility requirements) justify it.

items.prompt: A team builds a separate container image per environment (one for dev, one for staging, one for prod), each with its own baked-in config and secrets. What failure mode does this reproduce?
choices: None — this is exactly the recommended parity pattern

It reintroduces the exact drift risk containers exist to remove, just one layer up — instead of one artifact run everywhere with config injected at run time, there are now multiple artifacts that can independently diverge
This is only a security risk, not a parity risk
It's a performance problem only, since building multiple images takes longer
items.explanation: The correct pattern is one artifact, config injected at run time (docker run -e, or an orchestrator's config) — baking environment-specific config into separate images per environment recreates the same 'these are supposed to be the same but independently drifted' problem the container was supposed to solve.
items.reference:
SymptomFailure mode
Prod config found inside the imageBaked-in secrets/config
Same tag, different bytes than last weekTag pinned, not digest pinned
items.learnMore:
Four failure modes, one root cause

Every failure mode here comes from letting something outside the reviewed, versioned artifact affect behavior — a mutable tag, a re-resolved dependency, an environment-baked secret, or an assumption that parity covers a system boundary it doesn't.

Common mistake

Treating these as four unrelated Dockerfile nitpicks instead of four instances of the same underlying mistake: letting something outside the built artifact influence what actually runs.

They only matter for very large images, not small ones

items.prompt: A reviewer flags a Dockerfile because its FROM line has no tag at all (just `FROM node`). Why is that worth flagging, given the failure modes covered in this unit?
choices: It isn't worth flagging — an untagged image reference is a harmless shorthand for the most recent stable release

An image reference with no tag implicitly defaults to `:latest`, which carries the exact same repointing risk as writing `:latest` explicitly — it's the same failure mode, just easier to miss in review
It's only a style issue, unrelated to any of the failure modes covered
Docker refuses to build an image with an untagged FROM line, so this would never actually happen
items.explanation: Omitting a tag is functionally identical to writing :latest explicitly — Docker fills in the default silently, which is precisely why it's easy for a reviewer to miss compared to an explicit :latest that at least announces itself.

items.prompt: Write `isUnpinnedBaseImage(fromLine)` — a small review-automation check that flags a Dockerfile's `FROM` line as unpinned if it references `:latest` explicitly, OR omits a tag entirely (which Docker defaults to `:latest`). A line pinned to any other explicit tag, or pinned by content digest (`@sha256:...`), should NOT be flagged.

tests.description: a specific version tag is not flagged
no tag at all is flagged (implicit latest)
a digest pin is not flagged, even without a tag

items.explanation: The check has to handle three cases correctly: a digest pin is always safe regardless of tag; a missing tag is exactly as risky as an explicit :latest, since Docker fills it in silently; and any other explicit tag is fine. Splitting on '/' before checking for ':' matters because a registry host can itself contain a port (e.g. myregistry.io:5000/node) that would otherwise be mistaken for a tag separator.
items.reference: A base image string ending in :latest, or with no tag at all, is the check to flag in review.
items.learnMore:
Catching a parity risk before it ships

A base image reference with no tag defaults to :latest implicitly, which is exactly as unstable as writing :latest explicitly — both make "same Dockerfile" stop meaning "same bytes" over time. A lint-style check for this is cheap and catches the mistake before a build, not after an incident.

Common mistake

Forgetting that omitting a tag entirely is the same risk as writing :latest explicitly — Docker defaults to latest silently.

items.prompt: Write `isUnpinnedBaseImage(fromLine)` — same rule as before (flag `:latest` or no tag; allow any other explicit tag or a digest pin) — but it must also work correctly when the base image includes a registry host with its own port number, like `myregistry.io:5000/node:20.11`, without mistaking the registry's port for a missing tag.

tests.description: a registry host with a port, plus a real tag, is not flagged
a registry host with a port, but no image tag, is flagged
a plain image with :latest is flagged
a plain image with a real tag is not flagged

items.explanation: Splitting on '/' and taking the last segment before checking for ':' is what correctly separates "a registry host's port number" from "the image's tag" — myregistry.io:5000/node has a colon in the registry portion, but the tag check only ever looks at the final path segment, so it correctly sees 'node' as untagged rather than being fooled by the port.
